claims.text: Applying moderate external pressure enhances electron–phonon coupling and induces superconductivity in the selected high-entropy alloy at cryogenic temperatures.
Adding a minor tailored alloying element enhances electron–phonon coupling and induces superconductivity in the selected high-entropy alloy.
The selected alloy is non-superconducting in its as-cast state at ambient pressure and low temperature.
The as-cast selected alloy has a disordered solid-solution structure.
Pressures up to a few tens of GPa constitute an appropriate moderate intervention range.
An alloying addition of about 1 wt.% or less can locally distort the lattice.
An alloying addition of about 1 wt.% or less can enhance electron–phonon interactions.
The intervention produces local lattice distortions and altered electronic inhomogeneities in the disordered HEA matrix.
Local lattice distortions and altered electronic inhomogeneities modify the effective electron–phonon coupling.
Enhanced electron–phonon interactions facilitate Cooper-pair formation.
The intervention tips the initially non-superconducting alloy into a superconducting phase.
The modified sample will exhibit a measurable superconducting transition with a defined critical temperature.
The modified sample will exhibit stronger electron–phonon coupling than the baseline sample.
Moderate pressure or minor alloying will preserve the HEA's single-phase disordered structure.
Interventions beyond several tens of GPa or about 1 wt.% alloy addition may cause phase transformations or other extraneous effects to dominate.
The magnitude of the critical-temperature enhancement and coupling modification is uncertain because of the interplay of disorder and configurational entropy in HEAs.
High configurational entropy is expected to stabilize an HEA phase by reducing its Gibbs free energy.
A superconducting state can be operationally identified through a transition to zero electrical resistance.

contradictions.description: The central hypothesis requires the intervention to induce superconductivity, but the falsification rule requires both an absence of coupling enhancement and an absence of superconductivity. Thus, enhanced coupling without a superconducting transition would contradict the hypothesis and proposed mechanism but would not satisfy the stated falsification rule.
